The Iraqi government wants oilfields in the semi-autonomous Kurdistan region owned by the federally-held North Oil Company to be placed under federal control after uncovering oil smuggling in the northern fields, Iraq’s Oil Minister, Basim Mohammed Khudair, has said.
“An investigation has been conducted, the findings of which will yield specific recommendations. There have been violations at oil fields belonging to the North Oil Company,” Khudair told Iraqi News Agency INA in an interview , referring to the uncovering of oil-smuggling operations.
The fields belonging to the North Oil Company “have been seized” by the Kurdistan Regional Government (KRG), in addition to smuggling activities originating from other areas, the minister said.
The Iraqi Ministry of Oil believes that “the management of these fields should be federal, under the Ministry’s authority, consistent with how it manages fields in the central and southern regions,” Khudair told INA.
“The Prime Minister intends to resolve all outstanding issues and strengthen control over external border crossings by tasking the Iraqi Army with overseeing them, from the north to the south.”
The new showdown with the semi-autonomous region of Kurdistan is brewing just as Iraq is drafting and discussing its federal 2027 budget. Every year, the budget earmarks a share for the Kurdistan region.
For next year, the share for Kurdistan is kept at 12.5% of total spending in the budget.
But it also includes a provision that the KRG supply at least 400,000 barrels per day (bpd) of crude oil to Iraq’s State Oil Marketing Organisation (SOMO) for exports, according to the budget draft seen by Emirati news outlet The National . If KRG cannot export this volume, Kurdistan should deliver the crude to the federal ministry of oil for domestic use, per the budget draft.
Meanwhile, Iraq has boosted its crude oil exports via the Turkish Mediterranean port Ceyhan to 500,000 bpd, as OPEC’s second-largest producer has started trucking Basrah crude to the pipeline system to the north.

articles.title_orig: Exclusive | U.S. Prepares to Raise Tariffs on China and Other Countries
articles.title_zh: Exclusive | U.S. Prepares to Raise Tariffs on China and Other Countries
articles.content_orig:
US stock index futures are falling sharply following reports from The Wall Street Journal that the Trump administration is preparing another round of tariffs targeting China, the European Union, and 14 other economies. The proposed measures are intended to address excess industrial production capacity outside the United States, which Washington argues creates unfair competition and undermines American manufacturers. US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer could release the findings of a months-long investigation as early as this week, although the exact timing remains uncertain. S&P 500 futures have reacted with a sharp sell-off and are currently down nearly 1.5%.
The new tariffs could target a broad range of industrial goods imported from several major economies , including China, the European Union, Japan, South Korea, India, and Vietnam. Certain products, such as steel, aluminum, and automobiles, could be exempt because they are already subject to separate tariffs.
The Trump administration argues that foreign industrial subsidies contribute to overproduction, allowing companies to export goods at prices that make it difficult for American manufacturers to compete. The investigation is being conducted under Section 301 of the US Trade Act of 1974.
The exact tariff rates have not yet been officially determined. According to the WSJ, countries with existing trade agreements with the United States, including the EU, Japan, and South Korea, could face tariffs of no more than 15%, while China, India, and Vietnam may be subject to more restrictive measures.
The new tariffs could be imposed on top of existing import duties, increasing costs and complicating operations for businesses dependent on international supply chains. However, the final scope of the restrictions remains subject to decisions by the administration.
From a financial market perspective, the biggest concern could be the combination of higher import costs and persistent inflationary pressures in the United States. Additional tariffs could raise prices for components and finished goods, squeeze corporate profit margins, and complicate the Federal Reserve's efforts to bring inflation down. Industrial companies, electronics manufacturers, and retailers dependent on global supply chains would be particularly vulnerable.
For Wall Street, this raises the risk of a scenario in which slowing economic growth coincides with persistently elevated inflation. The extent of the threat will depend on the final tariff rates, the scope of exemptions, and the response from US trading partners. Today's WSJ reports do not mean that new tariffs have been formally introduced, but they are already increasing uncertainty surrounding the outlook for American businesses and global trade.
On the hourly chart, US500 has given back roughly one-third of yesterday's strong rebound. The sharp negative reaction highlights persistent nervousness across financial markets, while reports of potentially higher tariffs, including measures targeting China, appear to have introduced another source of risk for investors.
On the daily chart, a recovery above 7,400 points appears crucial for US500, as the 200-session exponential moving average (EMA200) is located near this level. For now, however, the index is struggling to generate sufficient buying momentum to initiate a sustained recovery. As long as it remains below this area, the risk of a continued downtrend persists. The key support zone lies between 6,900 and 7,000 points. A decisive breakdown below this range could expose the index to a deeper decline toward 6,300 points, corresponding to the lows recorded in spring 2026. Such a move would represent a correction of more than 20% from its all-time high.

articles.title_orig: Anthropic falls below $83 IPO price in swift reversal after record listing
articles.title_zh: Anthropic falls below $83 IPO price in swift reversal after record listing
articles.content_orig:
Oops, something went wrong
Just two days after its public debut, the stock market's newest AI giant, Anthropic ( ANT ), looks to be missing out on Monday's major tech rally.
Anthropic's stock briefly fell below its $83 IPO price during premarket trading on Tuesday, extending its slide. The stock fell 5% to $82.95 at 06:43 ET.
The stock of the Claude model maker fell 1.4% on Monday, trading below $88 as of 3:00 p.m. ET after whipsawing earlier in the day. Meanwhile, Nvidia ( NVDA ) and other AI-linked stocks, including CoreWeave ( CRWV ), soared amid the broader tech rebound that followed Jensen Huang's reinstatement as Nvidia CEO.
The move comes after Anthropic's stock sank 9% on Friday following a 17% gain on its IPO day last Thursday. At Monday's current price, the stock is up about 5% from its $83 IPO price.
Read more: What investors should know about buying into Anthropic stock
The choppy performance might reflect ordinary post IPO profit-taking and broader skepticism about Anthropic's valuation. Needham analysts said in a Sunday note that the most common concern they hear from investors is whether the company can sustain its enormous revenue growth next year. The company's fully diluted IPO valuation of about $1.5 trillion is roughly 40 times trailing sales.
The stock also has a potential supply overhang. As much as 315 million shares held by insiders, roughly one-third of the stock the company issued in its IPO, became eligible for sale almost immediately, according to Anthropic's IPO paperwork.
Needham added that given Anthropic's staggered schedule for permitting insider share sales could bring more shares to market in the first six months.
Another key question hanging over the company is how credit markets will absorb the AI firm's massive spending needs. Anthropic has committed to spending about $900 billion on its computing and infrastructure needs for the next two decades , including $70 billion due over the next 12 months.
The AI boom's ravenous capital needs have flooded the bond market this year, becoming a looming concern for investors.
Investors expect the major rating agencies to assign a high-yield, or junk, rating to the company's debt, according to a Wall Street Journal report . No rating has yet been announced.
Anthropic's credit rating is key for the wider AI ecosystem. Getting the higher investment-grade rating would help offer some relief to chip makers, including Nvidia and Broadcom ( AVGO ), that have guaranteed billions of dollars worth of microchips to customers that lease compute power to major model makers like Anthropic and rival OpenAI. ( OPAI.PVT )
The high-yield bond market also comes with constraints, including smaller capacity and higher borrowing rates, for the newly public giant.

articles.title_orig: One every four minutes: 720,000 Russian soldiers killed since start of Ukraine war, new data suggests
articles.title_zh: One every four minutes: 720,000 Russian soldiers killed since start of Ukraine war, new data suggests
articles.content_orig:
Almost three-quarters of a million Russian soldiers have been killed since Moscow launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, equating to roughly one death every four minutes, analysis based on leaked official data has revealed.
Russian opposition outlets Mediazona and Meduza reported on Monday that by the end of September, 490,000 Russian troops had been confirmed dead by Russia’s statistical bureau, Rosstat.
But accounting for time lags in reporting and including troops who have been reported as missing in action – and are most likely dead – Russian fatalities jump to more than 720,000 since the start of the war, according to the two outlets.
That is a staggering number that surpasses Russia’s death toll from the Soviet war in Afghanistan in the 1980s and both Chechen wars in the 1990s and early 2000s – and which the Kremlin has long tried to keep secret.
The Ukraine-Russia war is seeping out across Europe and there are two reasons it will get worse
Rosstat stopped publishing demographic data in 2025 to disguise the rising death toll from the war. Mediazona and Meduza, as well as other outlets, obtained the official data after two pro-Ukrainian hacker groups, Cyber ​​Partisans of Belarus and Silent Crow, managed to breach Rosstat’s servers earlier this month.
CNN cannot independently verify the figures, but the leaked data on confirmed deaths alone corroborates earlier estimates by analysts and Western intelligence – which now appear to fall far short of the likely real death toll.
Mediazona and Meduza have long been keeping a tally of Russian losses, based mostly on inheritance documents, death notices and other publicly available documents.
But the leaked Rosstat data allowed the media outlets to go a step further, using the same methods and calculations normally employed by actuaries estimating risks and insurance premiums.
By analyzing discrepancies between reported death dates and death registration dates, and by comparing these to search notices published by relatives, the reporters were able to extrapolate the number of deaths that have occurred but have not yet been reported to be somewhere around 230,000.
Mediazona has kept a tally of troops identified as missing by their relatives from 2023. That database contains 160,000 individuals and almost all of them are likely dead. Mediazona said that based on its reporting, the rate of survival among those reported missing only around 10%.
The data shared by Silent Crow showed that the war was the fourth most common cause of death in Russia since the start of the full-scale invasion, after heart diseases; Covid; and stroke and other vascular conditions. It also confirms what has long been suspected – that the losses are not spread evenly across Russia, with poorer areas and ethnic minorities suffering significantly higher casualty rates.
In addition, an analysis by the NEST Centre, a think tank that also obtained the data, revealed the scale of Russia’s recruitment of foreign fighters. It identified 6,947 records of foreign nationals killed in Ukraine – the majority of them from the central Asian countries of Kazakhstan, Uzbekistan, Tajikistan, Kyrgyzstan, and Turkmenistan.
Maria Pevchikh, the head of investigations at Alexey Navalny’s Anti-Corruption Foundation, said the release of the data shows why Russian President Vladimir Putin is unlikely to seek compromise to end the war.
Hours after Trump reportedly says ‘tired’ Putin is ready for a deal, Ukraine hit with massive strikes
“Putin has no way to ‘step back from public life’ or ‘focus on housing and utilities problems’ after killing 700,000 of his own citizens, and he never will. You don’t retire after something like that,” she said on X.
Meanwhile, Alexander Baunov, a senior fellow at the Carnegie Russia Eurasia Center, noted the war in Ukraine was Russia’s deadliest conflict since World War II.
“We talk a lot about the risk of nuclear escalation. But in terms of human losses, we may already be approaching the scale of a limited nuclear war,” he said.
Aby Shukiurov, a demographer and an associate fellow at the NEST Centre, said the Russian authorities “made concerted efforts to conceal the demographic reality of the war.”
Shukiurov pointed out that the high death toll has pushed down male life expectancy in Russia to 65.3 years in 2025. That is 3.1 years lower than in 2019 and almost at the level recorded in 2021, the worst year of the pandemic. Meanwhile, female life expectancy continued to rise during the war, reaching a record high of 79.3 years in 2025, he said.
Like Russia, Ukraine doesn’t release official casualty data, although Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky has publicly acknowledged the scale of losses in combat. The most recent research by the Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS) estimated in July that the country has endured between 525,000 and 625,000 casualties, including 125,000 and 150,000 fatalities.
Baunov said that the combined death between Russia and Ukraine could exceed 1 million.
“One million dead is an important psychological threshold. But if almost nobody in Russia knows that this threshold may have been crossed, it is as if it hasn’t been crossed at all,” he said on X.
CNN’s Clare Sebastian and Nathan Hodge contributed reporting.

articles.title_orig: Best Buy reports comparable sales growth of 6.1%, highest in five years
articles.title_zh: Best Buy reports comparable sales growth of 6.1%, highest in five years
articles.content_orig:
Best Buy on Tuesday beat Wall Street expectations on the top and bottom lines for its third fiscal quarter and raised its full-year guidance.
The consumer electronics retailer reported comparable sales growth of 6.1%, a significant beat over expectations of 2.3%, according to market intelligence platform StreetAccount. The company said that growth was its highest in five years. It reported a domestic comparable sales increase of 6.2% and international comparable sales growth of 4.9%.
Shares of Best Buy climbed 6% following the report .
Best Buy also raised its guidance for the rest of the year. It's now expecting full-year revenue of between $43 billion and $43.3 billion compared with a previous expectation of between $42.3 billion and $42.8 billion. It's expecting comparable sales to be up 3.4% to 4% compared with prior guidance of between 1.9% and 3%.
The earnings report is the company's first since Jason Bonfig took over as CEO from Corie Barry at the beginning of the month.
"Disciplined execution, a compelling product cycle and continued market share gains helped drive broad-based topline momentum across nearly all product categories, our services offerings, and both our digital and store channels," Bonfig said in a statement about the most recent quarter.
Here's how the company performed in the period ended Oct. 31 compared with what Wall Street was expecting, based on a survey of analysts by LSEG:
Best Buy reported net income of $353 million, or $1.66 per share, compared with $140 million, or 66 cents per share, the year prior. Adjusting for one-time items, including restructuring charges, Best Buy posted adjusted earnings of $1.62 per share.
Revenue rose to $10.24 billion from $9.67 billion in the year-ago period. Best Buy reported domestic revenue of $9.42 billion and international revenue of $820 million.
Tuesday's earnings are the latest in a series of strong reports from the retailer, which has been instituting a turnaround strategy to return to growth after getting hit by declining foot traffic, lower consumer sentiment, tariffs and memory costs .
Shares of Best Buy are up nearly 45% this year.
Bonfig told CNBC last quarter that the launch of " Grand Theft Auto VI " in the current quarter is expected to drive sales in the gaming category, which has been seeing gains over the past year. Last month, Best Buy launched a new gaming experience for customers featuring gaming content, technology and special offers, among other features.

articles.title_orig: China sentences official to death for spying for foreign country
articles.title_zh: China sentences official to death for spying for foreign country
articles.content_orig:
China has sentenced a government official to death for handing over state secrets and classified documents to a foreign intelligence agent.
In a public post, Monday, China’s National Administration of State Secrets Protection said the convicted official was approached and recruited by a foreign woman while working overseas.
It is extremely rare for China to disclose that it has sentenced someone to death for espionage, or publish details on proceedings involving national security.
The post did not mention where the official was posted, but gave his surname as Ma, and said he had been approached by a woman named ‘Kailin,’ who initially said she was interested to learn Chinese. It did not say what the woman’s nationality was.
After their relationship developed, ‘Kailin’ began shifting their chats to “politically sensitive” topics and major international developments, and convinced Ma to hand over sensitive information about the personnel and operations of a Chinese institution in the country, according to prosecutors.
Kailin later introduced Ma to her other colleagues and told him that if he did not become an agent for their country, they would tip off the Chinese government about his activities. Ma then signed a pledge of loyalty, starting down the path “being consumed by darkness, and doomed beyond redemption,” the statement said.
The official later returned to China and sent “hundreds” of classified intelligence documents to the foreign agent in return for a fixed monthly income with additional bonus when he provided key material, according to the statement.
China’s prosecutor found Ma sent nine documents classified as state secrets and 26 documents classified as confidential in return for more than $150,000 for the espionage activities.
The state secrets administration’s post offered a stern warning to Chinese citizens to “maintain vigilance in our social and personal lives, adhere strictly to workplace discipline, and guard against being targeted, manipulated or exploited by hostile actors.”
The verdict comes as China steps up its anti-espionage efforts as its strategic rivalry with the US-led west deepens.
In 2023 China broadened the scope of its already sweeping counter-espionage law to expand the definition of espionage from covering state secrets and intelligence to any “documents, data, materials or items related to national security and interests,” without specifying specific parameters for how these terms are defined.
Earlier this year its spy agency warned that China’s young people were being duped by foreign forces into shirking hard work and prioritizing their individual emotions at the expense of national development.
The post from the State Security Ministry’s official account warned young people to stay vigilant against “complex opinion traps” and any “lying flat” narratives that propagate the message that hard work is futile.

By JON MICHAEL RAASCH, WHITE HOUSE CORRESPONDENT
Published: 10:10 EST, 23 November 2026 | Updated: 06:09 EST, 24 November 2026
President Donald Trump has revealed what he told Jensen Huang right before the Nvidia chief executive was reinstated, following a 'spy' sex scandal that had forced him to resign.
'I talked to him [Jensen Huang] last night,' Trump told CNBC in an interview. 'I said, 'Jensen, just promise me one thing: You're going to work hard.
'You got brain, you got everything going. You're going to work hard, and if you work hard, there's nobody can beat you'.'
Nvidia's board of directors announced on Monday that the recently ousted boss would return to his position at the helm of the AI giant.
It prompted a stunning rally in Nvidia's shares – adding more than 30 per cent or nearly $1trillion (£763billion) to its value.
'The NVIDIA Board of Directors has made the correct and proper decision to return Jensen Huang to the position of CEO,' Trump wrote on social media.
The White House confirmed that Trump called in to the company's board of directors to advocate for Huang's return to leadership.
Huang's whirlwind firing and rehiring after multiple reported affairs, two with Nvidia subordinates and another with an alleged Chinese spy named Alice Huang, have prompted a tumultuous few weeks for the AI firm and the US economy .
'The Country needs Jensen's leadership at NVIDIA in order to ensure the Success and Prosperity of not only the Company, but the American Economy,' Trump said in a statement shortly after the company announced Huang's rehiring
Huang's whirlwind firing and rehiring after multiple reported affairs - two with Nvidia subordinates and another with an alleged Chinese spy named Alice Huang - have prompted a tumultuous few weeks for the AI firm and US economy
Trump posted a meme on his Truth Social showing Huang holding up a red bra in a wild re-imagining of the iconic photo after Trump was shot by a would-be assassin in 2023
'He's apologized for indiscretion, which was unfortunate. That was probably that's what brought it to such a level, because sex sells fellas!' Trump said in a CNBC interview Monday morning.
'Now, [Jim] Cramer would not know that because he's a very, very, very committed person. But sex sells.'
Trump also claimed that Huang's wife, Lori, 64, has also decided to stand by her husband despite his infidelity.
'He's got a very, very, very good wife, and they've worked it out,' Trump told The New York Times. 'She's a fantastic woman.'
The president separately posted a meme on his Truth Social showing Huang holding up a red bra in a wild re-imagining of the iconic photo after Trump was shot by a would-be assassin in 2023.
Huang met his wife of 41 years at Oregon State University, when they were paired as lab partners in an electrical engineering class. He was 17 at the time.
The couple had already welcomed their two children, Madison and Spencer, by the time he co-founded Nvidia in 1993.
Both Madison and Spencer now hold key positions within high-priority business units at the company.
Lori is the president of the family's $9 billion charitable foundation and often accompanies her husband to events.
As the US's predominant AI company and microchip manufacturer, Nvidia has ballooned to become one of the most expensive US companies and a leader of cutting-edge computational development in the race against China for tech supremacy.
The recent string of damaging stories about Huang's personal conduct contributed to the company hemorrhaging over $1 trillion in market cap.
But the stock roared back to life, gaining over 25 percent on Monday following Trump's announcement that the company is not a national security risk.
'The Country needs Jensen's leadership at NVIDIA in order to ensure the Success and Prosperity of not only the Company, but the American Economy,' Trump said in a statement shortly after the company announced Huang's rehiring.
'The United States Government has no reason to believe that Jensen's return to NVIDIA poses any risk to National Security.

'The Attorney General of the United States has confirmed that the U.S. Government does not possess evidence that he has engaged in any unlawful conduct.'
Huang is still the subject of an internal Nvidia investigation into his affair with Alice Huang, a former executive at Singapore-based data firm Megaspeed, which has been of particular concern within the administration.
There are suspicions that Alice Huang used her role at Megaspeed to convince the Nvidia boss to allow the sale of advanced chips to the Singapore-based firm before those same chips were used by Chinese AI firms, helping them effectively circumvent an export ban.
US officials noted that the Megaspeed executive speaks English well and has relationships with executives at the highest levels of the AI chip industry
'NVIDIA should continue its thorough internal investigation of the Company's compliance with U.S. export controls in order to ensure that it is fulfilling its legal obligations and Patriotic Duty to protect U.S. National Security,' Trump said.
Nvidia said in its announcement on Monday that the probe into the 'foreign intelligence effort' will proceed and that the CEO 'fully supports the investigation and is committed to cooperating with it.'
Additionally, the Nvidia boss is scheduled to testify before Congress on December 1 about the affair with the suspected spy.
The company has since established a national security and export control committee to identify possible compliance and security risks.
Trump has grown close with the Nvidia boss during his second term, repeatedly hosting Huang at the White House for ritzy state dinners and inviting him on state visits to China and the United Kingdom.
The president has also traded millions worth of Nvidia stock.
The Republican has made at least 108 transactions worth between $27.2 million and $97.9 million during his second term, according to a CNBC analysis of the president's Nvidia stock trades.
His official filing puts his Nvidia holdings at anywhere between $12.5million to $58million (£10million to £45million) at the end of 2025. The White House always says independent managers run Mr Trump's portfolio.
Huang returned Monday to Nvidia headquarters in Silicon Valley, and employees gathered in the building's atrium loudly cheered him on.
'I am going to be a better CEO the second time around,' Huang said.
The CEO, who will also serve as Nvidia president, said in a statement that he was 'honored' to return to the company and that he resumes the responsibility 'with the greatest humility and renewed commitment.'
He thanked board Chairman Harvey C Jones and interim CEO Colette Kress, who will return to her role as chief financial officer, as well as Nvidia's executive staff for their leadership during the brief period of disorder.
'I am also deeply thankful to our employees, shareholders, leaders across the industry and partners around the world for their extraordinary support,' Huang´s statement said.

articles.title_orig: Why are Russian warships off Libya, and will Ukraine’s attack change that?
articles.title_zh: Why are Russian warships off Libya, and will Ukraine’s attack change that?
articles.content_orig:
A Russian warship was sunk by Ukrainian drones at a port in Libya on Sunday, President Volodymyr Zelensky has said.
There was an explosion on the warship at the Benghazi naval base in the early morning, while it was docking for fuel and supplies ahead of its return to Russia, local authorities said.
Zelensky added that Ukraine's attack hit a second Russian vessel, a cargo ship which he claimed was being used to transport weapons.
The local health ministry said it had received injured people from a commercial ship that was targeted off the coast of the port. It is not clear whether this is the same vessel as the one Ukraine has claimed responsibility for.
Following the strikes, the Kremlin warned of an "escalation of tensions in the region", but declined to comment directly on the attacks in Libya.
Libya's two governments - the UN-recognised government in the capital, Tripoli, and a rival administration in the east - have both condemned the attack.
The Tripoli foreign ministry said the country would not accept being drawn into the conflict.
It said foreign forces would not be allowed to use Libyan ports and civilian infrastructure for military purposes.
The eastern government, based in Benghazi, called it a violation of maritime safety and an attack on their sovereignty.
Seven naval drones were deployed to target and sink the corvette Merkury, one of Russia's newest ships, Zelensky said in a statement on Monday. He added that a Ka-27 combat helicopter was also destroyed.
The Ukrainian president said the second ship was the MV ANGARA, a Russian container carrier.
The attack came the day after a Russian cargo vessel was hit by a drone attack in the eastern Gulf of Finland . The Sparta II had been bound for Russia's Baltic exclave Kaliningrad when it was hit on Saturday morning.
Finnish defence forces said Ukraine was likely to be behind the attack. Kyiv has not commented.
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov told reporters on Monday that the "expansion of terrorist activity in the Baltic" was a "dangerous trend" and has said "it is, of course, leading to an escalation of tensions in the region."
When questioned over the attacks in Libya, Peskov said information would be provided by the country's defence ministry and added: "We paid attention to Zelensky's statements about it".
Peskov declined to comment on the strikes on Russian ships in Libya and said that that information would be provided by Russia's Defence Ministry.
The UN mission in Libya expressed "serious concern" over the attacks on Sunday, calling for "an immediate, independent and transparent investigation".
"Libya cannot afford, and must not become a battleground for foreign conflicts," the UNSMIL wrote on X.
Videos posted on social media and geolocated by BBC Verify show the ship that was struck in the morning engulfed in flames and smoke. Satellite imagery from Planet Labs PBC also shows a boat on fire at 05:47 GMT at the Benghazi port.
US-based intelligence firm Vantor collected high-resolution images that it said showed Project 20380 Steregushchiy-class corvette (Merkury) - a Russian navy ship - moored in the port on Saturday, and on Sunday showed most of the same ship capsized and sunk with only the forward bow still visible.
Neither of Libya's rival administrations has formally declared support for either side in the Russia-Ukraine war, but they have contrasting ties with Moscow and Kyiv.
The head of the Libyan National Army, which controls much of the east of the country, has longstanding links with Russia.
The eastern-based Government of National Stability (GNS) said the Russian ship - which it did not name or identify - was using the Benghazi port within the framework of an existing maritime agreement.
Sunday's incident is under investigation, and authorities are coordinating with their Russian counterparts to determine the source of the suspected attack and who is responsible for it, GNS added.
It said Libya was not party to the Russia-Ukraine war, or any other conflict beyond its borders.
GNS has accused the Tripoli-based Government of National Unity (GNU) of hosting Ukrainian military personnel and allowing them to operate from Libyan territory against Russian targets.
Separately, the GNU warned against hosting foreign forces and allowing them to use facilities in a statement published by state media.
It said such activity raises "serious fears" about "risks that may result from involving ports and civilian facilities in activities related to external conflicts, and the resulting threat to the lives of citizens and the safety of national facilities and assets".
Libya fractured into violence and instability after its leader Muammar Gaddafi was overthrown in 2011, leading to the opposing governments.
Benghazi is more than 2,000 km (1,243 miles) away from the Russian capital Moscow.
In March, Russia accused Ukraine of targeting the Russian tanker Arctic Metagaz in the Mediterranean between Libya and Malta with "uncrewed sea drones" launched from the Libyan coast.
As well as having an economic impact on Russia, hampering the ability of their so-called shadow fleet of tankers to export oil and gas, attacks like this are seen as humiliating to the Kremlin, according to Dr Jalel Harchaoui of the Royal United Services Institute (RUSI).
But it is not only Moscow that will want to react to this latest incident. The ship was in the region as part of a deal with the government of eastern Libya - allied with Khalifa Haftar, commander of the Libyan National Army.
Harchaoui said Haftar will take the attack as a personal slight. "You're going to have a response by the Haftar family. They will ask questions about who is hosting the Ukrainians."

articles.title_orig: Stock futures decline as Nvidia pulls back, giving back part of Monday’s rally: Live updates
articles.title_zh: Stock futures decline as Nvidia pulls back, giving back part of Monday’s rally: Live updates
articles.content_orig:
Nvidia's remarkable stock comeback isn't done yet now that Jensen Huang has returned as CEO , CNBC's Jim Cramer said Monday.
"It's terrific to have this admittedly tarnished national treasure back leading Nvidia," the " Mad Money " host said. "It's kind of a miracle given the board's insistence that he would never get the CEO job again. But it's a miracle that saved the Nasdaq which, in turn, saved the market, at least for now."
Nvidia shares soared 31.5% on the news, fueling a broader rally in AI infrastructure stocks. The S&P 500 jumped 4.7%, while the tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite surged 6.5%, with both indexes posting their best days since April 2025. Monday's rebound erased nearly all of Nvidia's decline following Huang's Nov. 12 resignation amid reports of multiple extramarital affairs, including one involving an alleged Chinese spy. Before the rally Monday, the stock had fallen in all trading sessions since his departure.
"Jensen's only one man, and Nvidia is only one company," he said. "But the truth is that Jensen is the linchpin that holds the AI solar system together, and Nvidia is the biggest beneficiary."
Cramer argued that Huang's reinstatement removes a major source of uncertainty for investors, strengthening the case for a higher valuation. The chipmaker delivered blockbuster quarterly results last week, raising its revenue growth outlook to 75%, but the results did little to stem the sell-off as investors remained concerned about its leadership.
"If it weren't for the Jensen overhang, and the insistence that Jensen could never come back, ... I think the stock would have been up significantly on that quarter," Cramer said.
Still, Cramer cautioned that Huang's return doesn't erase the broader headwinds facing Nvidia. Growing political opposition to data center construction following the midterm elections could slow AI infrastructure expansion, while uncertainty surrounding chip sales to China threatens a potential source of demand. Meanwhile, a more hawkish Federal Reserve has pressured technology stock valuations as investors brace for higher interest rates.
Those challenges, Cramer argued, make it difficult to justify a return to the $213 level Nvidia traded at before The New York Times first reported about Huang's relationship with a woman suspected of ties to Chinese intelligence on Oct. 29. But with Huang back at the helm and the company's growth outlook intact, he said the stock deserves a higher valuation. The stock currently trades at roughly 10 times earnings estimates for Nvidia's fiscal 2028, according to FactSet.
"There is just no way that, with the return of Jensen, this stock deserves the same 10 times price to earnings multiple," Cramer said.
"These things are subjective, of course, but to start, let's say this stock deserves to trade at twelve times next year's earnings estimate, which would make this a $199 stock," Cramer said. "That's my target."

articles.title_orig: A 74-year-old man with Alzheimer's survived 11 days lost in the Amazon rainforest: he built himself a shelter with palm leaves
articles.title_zh: A 74-year-old man with Alzheimer's survived 11 days lost in the Amazon rainforest: he built himself a shelter with palm leaves
articles.content_orig:
A former gold prospector was rescued alive in Macapá, in northern Brazil
An elderly Brazilian man with Alzheimer's has been at the center of a survival story that has astonished his rescuers. After spending more than a week and a half alone deep in the Amazon rainforest , he was found alive when his family had already feared the worst.
Janarino Ferreira dos Santos , 74, was found on Friday, November 20, in an area of dense vegetation on Ilha Redonda , in Macapá, the capital of the state of Amapá , in northern Brazil . He was about 10 kilometers from the point where he was last seen. His relatives saw him heading into the forest, but were unable to stop him.
Firefighters, forest rangers, relatives, and volunteers took part in the search . When the authorities were planning to suspend the operation on Sunday the 22nd, his granddaughter, Sara Monte, appealed on Instagram for them not to give up the search. Two days before that date, the teams found him. Weakened, he had to be carried out of the thick vegetation on an improvised stretcher. Images of the rescue show him sitting in his underwear and looking disoriented.
The key to his survival lay in his past. Former gold prospector , Janarino knew the jungle well. According to the rescuers, he fed on the fruits of the buriti, an Amazonian palm tree, and drank water from springs and small streams.
Forest ranger Nerivan da Silva explained that they found several beds the elderly man had made with açaí palm leaves to rest, as well as footprints indicating that he walked in circles. In one of those shelters they noticed a strong smell of urine, a detail that matched the urinary problems the family had described and that helped confirm his trail.
He is now recovering in a hospital in Macapá, where doctors are conducting tests and he is receiving treatment for a urinary tract infection. According to his granddaughter, he has dry skin, scratches, and thorns embedded in his feet.

articles.title_zh: Zelenskyy Confirms Ukraine Hit Russian Ship in Gulf of Finland
articles.content_orig:
A Russian cargo ship struck by drones in the Gulf of Finland has left Finnish territorial waters after posing a “serious danger” there, according to Finland’s President Alexander Stubb.
Stubb said late on Sunday that Finland would continue working to maintain stability and security in the Gulf of Finland and thanked the authorities for their response to Saturday’s incident.
Finland’s military said the strike on the Sparta II on Saturday was likely carried out by Ukraine and that the vessel later drifted into Finnish waters, where it was previously anchored. The 16 crew members were evacuated onto a nearby Russian ship.
A fire aboard the Sparta II continued to burn through the night despite efforts to extinguish it, the Finnish coastguard said.
“Unfortunately, the consequences of Russia’s war of aggression are also visible in our region,” Stubb said on X.
Pictures and video released by the coastguard on Sunday showed several vessels spraying the Sparta II with water cannon overnight to put out the flames and cool down containers stacked on its deck.
Ukraine has sent waves of military drones towards Russia’s northwestern coastal region of Leningrad this year, including some that strayed into the airspace of nearby Baltic countries, leading to fears that the war was spilling onto NATO territory.
The ship, bound for the Russian exclave of Kaliningrad, was damaged in international waters west of Russia’s Gogland Island, the Finnish Defence Forces said, corroborating an account by Russian officials.
Finland’s Prime Minister Petteri Orpo suggested the incident was related to Russia’s war on Ukraine.
“War is spilling over into our immediate vicinity … Ukraine has the right to fight back against the aggressor,” Orpo said on X.
The risk of further attacks in the Gulf of Finland, a narrow arm of the Baltic Sea, cannot be ruled out, Estonian Navy Commander Ivo Vark told public broadcaster ERR on Sunday.
Finland’s military said last week that it had detected a strike on a Russian warship in the same area during Ukrainian drone attacks.
The Sparta II is a 121-metre (397-foot) Russian-flagged cargo vessel owned by Russian shipping company Oboronlogistika that left St Petersburg on Friday, according to data from the London Stock Exchange.
The vessel is subject to United States sanctions, according to the US Department of the Treasury.
Oboronlogistika provides logistics services for the Russian Ministry of Defence, according to the company’s website.

articles.title_orig: Bangladesh’s ousted leader Hasina plans to return home from exile on Dec 16
articles.title_zh: Bangladesh’s ousted leader Hasina plans to return home from exile on Dec 16
articles.content_orig:
Sheikh Hasina, the former prime minister of Bangladesh who was overthrown more than two years ago, plans to return home from exile in India on December 16, her spokesperson said, as the government said she can only return through extradition.
Hasina went into exile in August 2024 after a student-led mass uprising forced her to end her 15-year rule.
She was later sentenced to death by a Bangladesh court in her absence for ordering the deadly crackdown on the uprising in which hundreds of protesters were killed.
Hasina rejected the verdict and has said she is ready to fight the case once she is back.
Announcing her plan to return on the anniversary of the end of her country’s 1971 liberation war with Pakistan , she urged Prime Minister Tarique Rahman to arrange her flight on the national airline.
“Since Sheikh Hasina was flown to India on a Bangladesh aircraft on August 5, 2024, she now calls upon the government to arrange for her air transport from Delhi back to Dhaka,” spokesperson Syed Mozammel Ali said in a statement on Tuesday.
Abu Abdullah M Saleh, Prime Minister Rahman’s press secretary, told the Associated Press news agency that the government would stick to its position on Hasina’s extradition as a convict.
“My government’s stand is very clear. She has been convicted in a tribunal. We have sought her extradition,” he said by phone.
Hasina is expected to be arrested upon her return and sent to jail.
Aminul Islam, chief prosecutor of Bangladesh’s International Crimes Tribunal, which sentenced Hasina to death, said it was unreasonable for a convicted fugitive to expect the government to arrange her return.
The judiciary had earlier said that Hasina would not be able to appeal her death sentence as she missed the required deadline and there would be no legal basis to stop her execution.
In Bangladesh, presidential clemency is allowed, but Hasina has never sought that in earlier statements and has rejected the verdict outright.
The United Nations has said as many as 1,400 people were killed during the unrest that forced Hasina from power.
Hasina’s father led the war against Pakistan and after independence was the first leader of the new People’s Republic of Bangladesh.
He was killed in a military coup in 1975, along with most of his family members. Hasina and her younger sister survived as they were out of the country.

articles.title_orig: Tiny Bahrain Is Paying a Big Price for Its Ties to the U.S.
articles.title_zh: Tiny Bahrain Is Paying a Big Price for Its Ties to the U.S.
articles.content_orig:
The Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) claimed to have targeted radars at a United States military base in Bahrain, as Iran has intensified attacks over the past week, hitting tankers in the Strait of Hormuz, a global oil chokepoint, and downing US drones.
At least 25 tankers have been hit in and around the Strait of Hormuz, through which a fifth of global oil and gas passes, in the past seven days, causing the Gulf oil flow to drop sharply.
The escalating attacks come as Iran’s President Masoud Pezeshkian said his country is facing what he called a “silent economic war” amid US sanctions and a naval blockade.
So what is behind Iran’s latest escalation, and will it trigger a new round of hostilities between Tehran and Washington or force the two sides to sit down for talks to end the war that has caused a global energy crisis?
Bahrain has faced the brunt of Iran’s attacks in recent days.
On Saturday, Manama said an Iranian strike hit a civilian industrial facility, starting a fire , as it thwarted several other attacks that day.
The IRGC said it had carried out a combined missile and drone operation targeting US military positions at the al-Riffa and Awali bases in Bahrain, claiming to have destroyed two US Patriot air defence radars at the bases.
Iranian state media reported that an interceptor missile launched from the US Fifth Fleet base in Bahrain crashed on Sitra Island near Manama, sparking a large fire.
The IRGC said the operation was retaliation for a US strike on a radar installation on Iran’s Hengam Island. Iran has justified the attacks as a response to continued violations of its airspace, including by US MQ-1 and MQ-9 reconnaissance and combat drones.
Bahrain has faced three drone attacks in recent days after a lull in fighting for several weeks.
Iran’s army on Saturday said its air defences fired a missile at a US F-16 jet over the Gulf the previous evening, damaging the aircraft, the IRNA news agency reported. However, US Central Command (CENTCOM) denied the claim, stating that “all US fighter jets in the Middle East are safe and accounted for”.
Iranian forces on Sunday also said they shot down another MQ-1 drone east of the Strait of Hormuz. The IRGC claimed it was the 20th US drone of this type to be shot down since the war began in late February and the fourth in the past 24 hours.
Meanwhile, British maritime authorities reported two incidents involving tankers struck by unidentified projectiles in the Strait of Hormuz near Oman.
Al Jazeera correspondent in Tehran, Resul Serdar, said incidents involving tankers had increased sharply over the past week, with about 25 since November 14.
Last week, the Iranian army also said it targeted US drone and missile installations at Kuwait’s Ali Al Salem base. The attack came after the US struck Qeshm Island in the Strait of Hormuz, which remains under effective Iranian control.
Oil passing through the Strait of Hormuz has seen a considerable dip as Iran has escalated attacks on a near-daily basis.
According to the UK Maritime Trade Operations (UKMTO), 263 ships passed through the key waterway between November 12 and 18, which is 15 percent fewer than the previous week and 20 percent fewer than the week before that.
Of those vessels, 37 were oil tankers, down from 52 the previous week, UKMTO reported on Friday.
The figures, however, could be higher as vessels passing through as part of shadow fleets are not officially registered.
About 135 ships passed daily through the vital strait before the war began in February.
Last week, the US maritime agency warned that the Iran blockade was adding to rising Gulf premiums, with insurance rates up from 0.10-0.25 percent before the war to 3.5-7.5 percent.
Oil prices have spiked, crossing $100 a barrel before settling down to $83, still more than $15 from before the war.
Cumulative losses from the conflict have now reached 2.8 billion barrels of oil and 60 billion cubic metres of gas supply from the Gulf, the International Energy Agency (IEA) said on Thursday.
The IEA, however, added that the conflict could cut world oil demand by more than 4 percent by 2035 if governments accelerate electrification, efficiency and fuel-switching measures in response.
As Iran has ramped up attacks, senior officials have asked the US to choose between surrendering to missiles or to diplomacy.
The attacks indicate that Iran is using its leverage in the conflict, sending the message that the US allies in the region will continue to bear the brunt of its actions if the war does not end.
The attacks aim to diminish US military capabilities in the region and “also to spread the pain of the war widely to include the entire [Gulf region] and, indirectly, global economies via higher shipping costs and stressed supplies of essentials”, Rami Khouri, a public policy fellow at the American University of Beirut, told Al Jazeera.
The single biggest driver of this strategy, Khouri said, is for Iran to continually ensure that it will no longer “suffer alone from US-Israel-imperial assaults”.
Tehran is hoping to change US policy by revealing its inability to protect its own facilities or those of its Arab allies, which could prompt Arab governments to press US President Donald Trump to end the war, Khouri, who is also a nonresident senior fellow at the Arab Center Washington DC, added.
Meanwhile, Deputy Foreign Minister Kazem Gharibabadi told Iranian media that he considers the economic blockade imposed by the US on Iran an act of war.
“We consider the economic siege a hostile act, and we will take any necessary measures to break this economic siege,” Gharibabadi told Iranian reporters.
The ongoing US naval blockade on Iran, overland trade disruptions and a wave of new sanctions imposed in August as part of Operation Economic Outcast are hurting Iran economically.
US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, who has led Washington’s sanctions regime against Tehran, has claimed the economic embargo will result in a 25 percent contraction of the Iranian economy by the year ending March 2027.
However, Iranian authorities insist they can withstand the economic pressure.
The strikes on US interests in the Gulf in recent days have therefore been viewed as a defiant response to the US campaign. But there are signs that the country’s economy and common Iranians are suffering from the current conditions.
Trump may choose to declare victory and walk away from the war on Iran rather than negotiate a deal, but continuing the naval blockade on Iran would risk further military escalation, says Trita Parsi, executive vice president of the Quincy Institute for Responsible Statecraft.
Speaking to Al Jazeera, Parsi said Trump was unlikely to accept an agreement that could be seen in Washington as showing the war had failed.
“If he continues the blockade, there will be escalation,” Parsi warned, arguing that Iran would not refrain from retaliating against continued economic pressure.
He said Trump would need to “slowly, perhaps imperceptibly, lift the blockade, as well as lift some of the sanctions” if he wanted to withdraw from the confrontation without renewed fighting.
Hassan Ahmadian, professor at the University of Tehran, said Iran is forcing a “binary” choice on Trump.
If Washington lets the tankers pass, the US blockade “ends without an agreement or war”, Ahmadian said on X. However, if the US attacks the vessels, it could face “Iranian responses that will be difficult for [Trump] to avoid”.
Trump said on Saturday he had plans to make a deal with Iran that is “permanent” and prevents it from getting a nuclear weapon.
He also told US broadcaster Fox News that he was never very interested in regime change in Iran, but called its new leadership “more rational”.

Oops, something went wrong
Colette Kress has been the CFO of Nvidia ( NVDA ) since 2013, helping to build the company at the center of the AI boom alongside founder and public face Jensen Huang.
She stepped into the line of fire for 12 days as interim CEO while Huang worked behind the scenes to return.
She withstood fresh reports of Huang berating her in meetings, and President Trump saying in an interview that she did a poor job in her post-earnings TV interview last week.
In the end, Nvidia's longtime CFO Colette Kress — a widely respected figure on Wall Street — has been left holding the bag.
And, apparently, left out of the loop on Huang's return.
"The talks that culminated in an Nvidia board meeting late on Sunday were so secretive that even interim chief executive officer Colette Kress was kept out of the discussions," a new report on Tuesday from the Financial Times said, citing people familiar with the matter.
An Nvidia spokesman didn't respond to Yahoo Finance's request for comment.
Shares of Nvidia fell nearly 4% in premarket trading on Tuesday after a 31.2% surge on news that founder Jensen Huang had been reinstated as CEO. That came just 12 days after he resigned amid a personal scandal and federal chip-export probes.
Kress is returning to the CFO role, though her LinkedIn profile still says interim CEO.
The dramatic reversal followed intense lobbying from President Donald Trump and Vice President JD Vance, who intervened directly with directors and said Huang had been cleared of national security concerns.
Upon returning to Nvidia's Silicon Valley headquarters, Huang promised employees he would be a better CEO the second time around.
Despite the rally , Nvidia still faces ongoing DOJ and SEC investigations into alleged chip smuggling through blacklisted Singapore-based firm Megaspeed, prompting the board to appoint a new chief compliance officer.

articles.title_orig: Roche says breast cancer pill could be best-selling drug ever
articles.title_zh: Roche says breast cancer pill could be best-selling drug ever
articles.content_orig:
Roche’s Wilserdly has become the first oral SERD approved by the FDA in early-stage breast cancer, kicking off the drug class’s biggest commercial test yet in a post-surgery market that holds the bulk of its multibillion-dollar sales potential.
The FDA has greenlit Wilserdly for the post-surgery adjuvant treatment of intermediate to high-risk estrogen receptor (ER)-positive, HER2-negative early-stage breast cancer. It marks the first new endocrine therapy option in this setting in more than two decades.
The landmark nod arrives just days after the agency approved Wilserdly alongside everolimus in previously treated, ESR1-mutated advanced breast cancer, making it the fourth oral SERD to reach the market.
The approval is backed by data from the phase 3 lidERA trial, which showed that Wilserdly cut the risk of invasive breast cancer recurrence or death by 30% compared with standard endocrine therapies—tamoxifen or aromatase inhibitors—achieving a three-year invasive disease-free survival rate of 92.4% versus 89.6%.
For Roche, the approval validates both a molecular design and a high-stakes clinical bet. Despite the estrogen receptor being a well-established target for decades, the field had gone more than 20 years without a new breakthrough in early breast cancer, which is a large population, Aviv Regev, head of Genentech Research and Early Development at Roche, said in an interview with Fierce ahead of the approval. Of about 225,000 U.S. patients diagnosed with HR+/HER2- breast cancer each year, nearly 90% are caught at an early stage.
To overcome the barrier, Genentech set out to engineer an oral pill that would achieve “a deeper inhibition and more sustained one” of the estrogen receptor, Regev said.
Guided by that goal, Genentech’s chemistry team designed a novel small-molecule scaffold in just eight months before moving rapidly into early-stage proof-of-concept studies that confirmed strong anti-proliferative activity compared with existing endocrine therapies and on-target receptor degradation. For the target, Roche found that Wilserdly “sticks on the chromatin, doesn’t allow it to move, changes its ability to execute its function, and eventually leads to its degradation,” Regev explained.
Rather than waiting for late-stage metastatic trial readouts, Roche launched lidERA in 2021 straight out of those early trials.
“That’s a very courageous move because a lot [of people] would want to first see” results in safer disease settings, Regev said, recalling a comment from a colleague around the time she joined Roche in 2020.
With a large patient population and expected long treatment duration, early-stage breast cancer represents the most important market for the oral SERD class. And Roche Pharmaceuticals CEO Teresa Graham has maintained that Wilserdly could become the largest-selling product in Roche’s history, even after it flunked a first-line metastatic trial.
While Wilserdly enjoys a first-mover advantage and is the only oral SERD to have a positive phase 3 readout in early breast cancer so far, commercial success is far from guaranteed. Since lidERA was launched in 2021, the adjuvant treatment landscape has been reshaped by CDK4/6 inhibitors, namely Eli Lilly’s Verzenio and Novartis’ Kisqali.
In an October note, Jefferies analysts suggested that the broad uptake of CDK4/6 inhibitors has shrunk the remaining commercial “white space” for oral SERDs. The remaining opportunity, Jefferies argued, “lies in patients who never initiate or complete CDK4/6 therapy, residual-risk patients after CDK4/6 exposure, biomarker-selected ultra-high-risk disease (e.g. ctDNA-positive MRD), and patients unable to tolerate prolonged CDK4/6 treatment.”
Although the lack of CDK4/6 involvement in the lidERA dataset so far represents a key weakness for Wilserdly, Regev emphasized that Roche mapped out a “multiplicity of trials that are done in parallel to each other” to evaluate the drug across different settings.
First up, a single-arm substudy of lidERA that combines Wilserdly with Verzenio is expected to read out this year, and a separate substudy is with Kisqali. Roche recently unveiled an investigator-initiated phase 3 study testing a ctDNA-guided treatment de-escalation approach and a Pfizer-led phase 1/3 to pair Wilserdly with the New York pharma’s CDK4 candidate atirmociclib.
Jefferies’ analysts compared Roche’s clinical program to AstraZeneca’s for its rival oral SERD Etcamah and argued that the latter has an upper hand. Between two phase 3 trials called Cambria-1 and -2, AZ is evaluating either switching patients to Etcamah after two to five years of prior endocrine-based therapy, which allows CDK4/6 treatment, or using adjuvant Etcamah upfront, including in tandem with a CDK4/6 drug.
Meanwhile, Lilly is running the Ember-4 switch trial for its oral SERD Inluriyo, and Menarini is testing Orserdu in a similar study.
Following a survey of 26 breast cancer specialists, Jefferies analysts noted that, even though Wilserdly currently leads physician perceptions, likely thanks to its unique phase 3 win in the adjuvant setting, physicians view the oral SERDs as having broadly similar efficacy and tolerability. “As a result, future adoption may depend increasingly on clinical positioning and [phase 3] design,” the analysts said.
Aditya Bardia, M.D., of UCLA Health, principal investigator of lidERA, suggested that for patients with lower-burden, lymph node-negative disease, where clinicians often hesitate to add the toxicity of a CDK4/6 inhibitor, Wilserdly monotherapy offers a compelling option.
“Now with the efficacy with oral SERD, with giredestrant, I think that does become a serious consideration whether you can just use a single agent,” he said.
Jefferies’ analysts suggested that initial uptake of Wilserdly in the adjuvant setting could come from CDK4/6-intolerant patients, even though existing clinical data do not directly address this population. Following the lidERA readout, respondents to Jefferies’ survey indicated that Wilserdly could be used in 44% of patients who drop off CDK4/6 therapy due to intolerance.
That’s not a small population. As Jefferies noted, in Novartis’ Natalee trial that got Kisqali approved in the adjuvant setting, 42.8% of patients completed the full three years of treatment, and most patients had discontinued by the data cutoff.
As to whether to combine a CDK4/6 inhibitor with an oral SERD upfront or sequence them for higher-risk patients, Bardia said he favors using the most potent endocrine agent from the start, although he noted the switch method has its own pros and cons.
Using an oral SERD later could theoretically prevent late recurrence or development of ESR1 mutations, Bardia said. However, some patients may develop recurrence early, and switching medication can be disruptive as patients have adjusted to their initial regimen’s side effects, he noted.
Keeping patients on treatment without disruption is key in the curative adjuvant setting, Bardia said. In lidERA, treatment discontinuation due to adverse events was lower with Wilserdly, at 5.3%, than with standard endocrine therapy, at 8.2%.
Based on its survey, the Jefferies team estimate risk-adjusted revenue for Wilserdly at 4.8 billion Swiss francs by 2034, mostly from the adjuvant setting, for which the analysts assigned a 50% probability of success. Current consensus estimates sit at 6.6 billion Swiss francs, according to Jefferies.
In Europe, Roche has delayed its filing for Wilserdly after European authorities encouraged the company to submit more mature overall survival data, which are expected by mid-2027, CFO Alan Hippe recently told Jefferies. As one analyst noted on Roche’s third-quarter earnings call in October, OS would make “a huge difference to some of the more skeptical docs.”

articles.title_orig: Sanofi Strikes $41 Billion Deal to Buy U.S. Drugmaker Insmed
articles.title_zh: Sanofi Strikes $41 Billion Deal to Buy U.S. Drugmaker Insmed
articles.content_orig:
Insmed shares rallied 14% in premarket trading Tuesday after Sanofi announced it would buy the smaller drugmaker for $41 billion, marking the largest pharma deal since 2023.
The acquisition includes Insmed's portfolio of two commercialized respiratory drugs as well as its pipeline of experimental candidates. Sanofi will pay $175 per share in cash.
It's a big bet by new Sanofi CEO Belen Garijo, who took up the role in May to steer the company through its upcoming patent cliff , when its blockbuster immunology drug Dupixent will face generic competition as patents expire.
If closed, the transaction will be the biggest one the industry has seen since Pfizer bought Seagen for $43 billion in December 2023.
Insmed shares rose 14.6% to $170.86 in early premarket trading, while Sanofi stock rose 6% in Paris.
Barclays analysts called the deal a "breath of fresh air," significantly improving Sanofi's Dupixent patent expiry outlook by adding Insmed's established respiratory assets Brinsupri and Arikayce, plus a late-stage pipeline offering further potential upside.
The deal is expected to close in the first half of 2027 and be accretive to earnings by the end of 2028, Sanofi said.
Like much of the industry, Sanofi faces a revenue drop towards the end of the decade as top-selling drugs lose exclusivity and open up for generic drugmakers to compete.
Global biopharma has experienced a sharp uptick in deals in 2026 , as the sector is driven by looming patent cliffs, newly buoyant public markets, and a race to beef up pipelines. Following a post-pandemic trough in 2022, M&A activity surged in 2025 and has accelerated into 2026.
While companies develop new medicines in-house, acquiring them is often faster and has become the go-to strategy for large biopharma companies with strong cash flows and financial firepower. Investors are also calling for sustainable revenue growth as major drugs lose exclusivity.
"Sanofi could offer a far more attractive investment opportunity given the significantly improved growth outlook," Barclays said in a note early Tuesday.
Formerly CEO at Merck KGaA , Garijo is facing pressure to find Sanofi's next growth driver. Her predecessor Paul Hudson stepped down earlier this year after the board chose not to renew his mandate , following a six-year reign during which his costly emphasis on R&D failed to deliver speedy results.
The Insmed deal is a good strategic fit that will help soften the blow from Dupixent's expected 2031–32 loss of exclusivity, said Jefferies analysts.
Insmed's medicines Brinsupri and Arikayce could add significant long-term revenue, with forecasts of $6.8 billion and $1.3 billion, respectively, in 2035, the analysts said. They see further potential upside if a settlement delays Dupixent's patent cliff, or if Brinsupri is included in Sanofi's alliance with Regeneron and positioned alongside Dupixent in respiratory diseases.
"The deal does not fix Sanofi's R&D/pipeline questions, but it buys time," the analysts said, adding that one potential wrinkle is future competition from AstraZeneca's tozorakimab, which is being studied for treatment in bronchiectasis, a chronic lung condition.
"Insmed builds on our already successful presence in respiratory diseases through its highly differentiated portfolio, strong science and proven commercial success," CEO Garijo said in a statement.
Sanofi shares fell 2.9%, and Insmed rose 24% on Nov. 19 after Bloomberg reported that a deal was underway.

articles.title_orig: Beyond Competition: How China's Automotive Transformation Is Creating New Global Opportunities
articles.title_zh: Beyond Competition: How China's Automotive Transformation Is Creating New Global Opportunities
articles.content_orig:
China's automotive transformation is creating a new set of industrial capabilities that could benefit the global automotive industry as a whole.
Over the past decade, China has developed a highly interconnected automotive ecosystem, bringing together battery technology, intelligent driving, vehicle software, advanced manufacturing, and an increasingly sophisticated supply chain.
The significance of this transformation lies not only in the competitiveness of Chinese automakers, but also in the opportunities these capabilities create for companies around the world.
Volkswagen offers an interesting example. The group is targeting annual exports of around 300,000 vehicles from China by 2030. More importantly, it plans to introduce China-developed vehicle platforms and electronic architecture into selected overseas markets，which represents a meaningful evolution in the role of China within multinational automakers' global operations.
Image source: Volkswagen Group China
For decades, international automotive companies brought technology, manufacturing expertise, management practices, and engineering capabilities to China. These contributions played an important role in the development of China's automotive industry.
Today, we are beginning to see industrial capabilities flow in the other direction as well.
Chinese companies are expanding their manufacturing, engineering, and supply-chain operations overseas. Meanwhile, multinational companies are increasingly integrating China's innovation resources into their global development strategies.
This is not simply a reversal of traditional globalization. It is an evolution toward a more interconnected model of industrial collaboration.
Different markets still have their own strengths. China's rapidly evolving technology ecosystem can complement Europe's engineering expertise, Japan's manufacturing and quality management capabilities, and the growing industrial capacity of emerging markets.
The opportunity is not to replicate the Chinese automotive model everywhere, but to combine complementary capabilities and develop solutions that meet different local needs.
Of course, this transformation brings challenges. Companies must navigate regulatory differences, cultural expectations, financial pressures, and increasingly complex localization requirements.
These challenges also highlight the importance of deeper industrial collaboration, local capability building, and disciplined long-term investment.
For global automotive executives, the strategic question should therefore extend beyond how to compete with Chinese companies. It should also be about how to leverage China's industrial capabilities, integrate them with existing strengths, and create better products and sustainable businesses for consumers around the world .
In my view, the greatest value of China's automotive transformation will not be measured solely by the number of vehicles Chinese companies sell globally. It will also be measured by how much this transformation contributes to the evolution of the entire global automotive industry.
That is a much greater opportunity than winning a car war.

articles.title_orig: China works to suppress India's rise across multiple fronts - USCC
articles.title_zh: China works to suppress India's rise across multiple fronts - USCC
articles.content_orig:
China is "actively working to suppress India's rise," even as the relationship between the two major Asian powers has thawed in the past year, according to a U.S. panel that sees an opening for greater outreach to India.
On Nov. 18, a U.S. China Economic and Security Review Commission report said Beijing is applying military, economic, maritime, and other forms of pressure to constrain India .
China has recalled engineers and withheld equipment to slow India's electronics manufacturing, slashed pharmaceutical input prices to undercut new Indian plants, and imposed export controls on battery technology to impede the development of India's clean energy industry, the report said.
It added that these tensions offer the U.S. an opportunity to counter growing Chinese influence by building closer ties with India across key sectors such as pharmaceutical and defense.
Ties have improved since a deadly border skirmish in 2020, but experts told CNBC that trust is still thin between Beijing and New Delhi. However, they added that the uneasy peace with China is unlikely to make India align automatically with the U.S. as an ally.
The Indian foreign and commerce ministries and the Chinese foreign ministry did not respond to emails seeking comments.
The thawing in relations between India and China came amid industrial demand, as well as the need for "a whole lot of posturing for the U.S.," said Arpit Chaturvedi, South Asia advisor at strategic advisory firm Teneo.
Over the past year, India faced tariff pressures and needed to signal to Washington that its options remain open, including that of renegotiating relations with China, he explained, but added that as the trade deal with the U.S. is "close enough now," there is no pressing need for that signaling.
Further improvement in the relationship is also limited by reports of renewed border tensions between the two sides and Beijing's scant reciprocation on easing access to technology and people movement, he said.
Last month, an Indian military official said that confrontations with Chinese soldiers were ongoing across several locations along the country's northeastern border, even as top leaders from the countries met with fanfare at the BRICS Summit in September.
Another flash point was when Beijing put export controls on tunnel boring machines last month. "Our relations with China remain good, and if there aren't any new hurdles , they can improve further," India's Commerce Minister Piyush Goyal reportedly said after China's move to tighten TBM exports.
On Monday, a Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesperson reportedly said Beijing is ready to work with India to facilitate visa arrangements for business personnel from both sides amid reports that fewer Indian businessmen got visas to attend an annual trade fair in Shanghai.
The Chinese "actively disrupt" areas where India is trying to make progress in terms of moving global supply chains, developing advanced industrial technologies such as EVs, batteries, electronic components, and pharmaceutical ingredients, Pramit Pal Chaudhuri, South Asia practice head at Eurasia Group, told CNBC.
He added China is increasingly focused on containing India economically rather than through military overtures.
India's manufacturing push still relies on Chinese inputs, from electronics components and solar materials to rare earth magnets and specialized machinery. Between April and October, India imported goods worth $96.6 billion from China , up more than 30% from a year ago, as per commerce ministry data released earlier this month.
Its major imports from China include electronic goods, machinery, chemicals, transport equipment, iron and steel, and pharmaceutical products.
While India needs inputs for its manufacturing ambitions from Beijing and China values access to Indian markets, trust between the two sides is "still thin," according to Reema Bhattacharya, head of Asia research at risk intelligence company Verisk Maplecroft, citing a large trade imbalance and overlapping interests in South Asia and the Indian Ocean as additional issues.

articles.title_orig: OpenAI and Cisco Unveil AI-Assisted Linux Security Tool to Block Exploits Before Patching
articles.title_zh: OpenAI and Cisco Unveil AI-Assisted Linux Security Tool to Block Exploits Before Patching
articles.content_orig:
OpenAI and Cisco have teamed up to launch Shirudo (meaning "shield" in Japanese), an open-source Linux runtime that allows artificial intelligence (AI) agents to defend systems without downtime.
"It lets agents write dynamic eBPF controls to shield systems from exploits, giving defenders more time to test and roll out patches," OpenAI said in a post on X.
The AI upstart called the initiative a "first step" toward "self-defending infrastructure" that can adapt itself to new threats while the services continue to run and enable defenders to test and deploy fixes without any disruption.
The development comes as AI is accelerating vulnerability discovery, finding critical bugs in foundational software used to power internet-connected software.
Shirudo is being pitched as a way for defenders to test temporary safeguards (aka shields) and check if they block behavior that exposes a vulnerability, while letting legitimate requests pass through. Once a shield is approved by an operator, it can be deployed without having to stop the service.
The idea is to avoid a complete service disruption to block a line of attack simply because both an exploit and a legitimate request may rely on the same underlying Linux operation.
To achieve this, Shirudo makes use of eBPF (short for extended Berkeley Packet Filter), a technology that makes it possible to run lightweight, sandboxed programs inside the kernel without the need for modifying the system code or restarting it.
"eBPF is a highly efficient, sandboxed virtual machine in the Linux Kernel," Cisco's Isovalent said . "These eBPF programs allow you to interact with the Linux kernel to observe and take action on any events happening on a machine. Some use eBPF to simply observe everything on their system, others use it to enforce policies (routing, security, and more)."
Notably, Shirudo is built atop the foundations of Tetragon , an eBPF-based security platform that Isovalent developed and open-sourced in May 2022. The crucial difference is that it's primarily designed for agents and leverages the capabilities of eBPF to inject code mitigations.
Central to Shirudo is a guardian agent that uses eBPF shields to block vulnerable code paths without restarting the system, while giving security teams the flexibility to monitor how a proposed shield would affect the application before enforcing it. The shields are also cryptographically signed and verified prior to being loaded.
"Agents scan open-source code and take in vendor disclosures," Cisco said. "They trace each vulnerability to the affected assets and attack paths, then write a small, targeted shield. They check that the shield covers the exploit and that the service still runs. The shield only graduates to active blocking when the evidence says it's safe, and it retires when the real patch lands."

In a controlled experiment, a Codex-generated shield blocked a Java4Shell exploit attempt against a running Elasticsearch service without requiring a restart, OpenAI said.
OpenAI and Cisco said the goal is to fight AI-based threats with AI and counter the risks posed by AI-driven attacks as soon as a vulnerability is identified at machine speed.
"We need this kind of machine-speed defense because AI models have become incredibly good at finding and exploiting software vulnerabilities, and they get better with every generation," Thomas Graf, CTO of Cisco Security, and Liz Rice, chief open source office at Isovalent, said. "They can also chain flaws together and discover creative new attack vectors that no one has thought about before."
"Yet a critical fix in widely-used software, from the Linux kernel to the libraries every application depends on, still takes days, weeks, or even months to reach the majority of systems. That timeframe is no longer acceptable given that the mean time to exploitation has become negative ."
